subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE OF $500 IN ANNUAL COMPENSATION OF CERTAIN EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement to the House on the subject of the wages and salaries of employees of the
government of Canada. As I said in this House the other day, the government has been giving this matter serious consideration. I am sure you are aware that an increasing number of employers across this country, as well as in most other industrialized countries, have been taking special action to adjust their employees' wages and salaries to meet the effects of unusual rises in costs. Since the first of this year, major employers outside the federal Public Service have, as a result, begun to adjust wage ranges, provide their employees with lump-sum payments, re-open wage agreements or adopt other measures to increase employee compensation.
The government of Canada has always had a policy of paying its employees at levels which compare fairly with those of other employers. We closely monitor pay movements outside the Public Service to maintain our position in this regard. In arriving at pay settlements with various groups of Public Service employees during the course of 1972, 1973 and the early part of 1974, both parties at the bargaining table relied on wages and salary data as to future increases outside the federal Public Service.

The government has concluded that it is inappropriate to deal with this development only through the process of collective bargaining as agreements come up for renewal. speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to table a working document entitled "A New Perspective on the Health of Canadians".
Mr. Speaker, in bringing this working document on health to the attention of the House, I would like to say a few words on why the document was prepared and on its significance.
Canadians traditionally rely upon the personal health care provided by hospitals, doctors, nurses, and other health professionals to protect them from diseases and death. While the importance of such personal health care is beyond question, Canadians should be aware of how they themselves could help safeguard and improve their own health by determining how their own chosen lifestyle and their environment affect both physical and mental well-being.
The need for a new perspective on health is evident from an examination of health data. Statistics show that the five most important causes of death before age 70, measured by potential years of life lost, are automobile accidents, coronary heart disease, other accidents, respiratory diseases-including lung cancer-and suicides.
Sickness treated in general hospitals shows a similar pattern. Measured by the days of hospitalization, the main causes of illness are coronary heart disease, all accidents, and respiratory diseases.
There is little doubt that improvements in the knowledge of the level of risks imposed by the lifestyle of individuals, of human biology and of environmental factors are important elements in helping to alter this pattern of disease and death.
The approach suggested in the working paper is to identify "high risk" segments of the Canadian population and to devise programs aimed at reducing these risks. By identifying the underlying causes and taking corrective action the health of hundreds of thousands of individuals can be safeguarded before disease is sufficiently far advanced as to require expensive medical care.
It is proposed, therefore, to divide the broad field of health into four basic elements. This division, which I outlined in a speech to the Pan-American Health Organization in September 1973 is referred to as the Health Field Concept. The first of the four elements of the concept is human biology. The second is the environment, next is lifestyle and, finally, health care organization. We also suggest a regulatory strategy consisting of eight proposals aimed at using federal regulatory powers to reduce health hazards and at encouraging and assisting provinces to use their regulatory powers to achieve this end. For the research strategy there are fifteen proposals designed to help discover and apply the knowledge needed to solve health problems. It is my hope that the possible courses of action suggested for the research strategy will enable the federal and provincial governments to jointly review research funding with a view to increasing their respective contributions.

May 1, 1974
Health
The health care efficiency strategy includes twenty-one proposals to assist the provinces in re-organizing their health care delivery systems so that cost, accessibility and quality are balanced in the best interests of all Canadians. Finally, the goal-setting strategy is made up of seven proposals to set, in cooperation with others, specific goals to be attained in improving the health of Canadians and in increasing the efficiency of health care systems.
Authority for the pursuit of these objectives is widely dispersed among governments, professions and organizations. Limitations on the availability of additional funds and differences of opinion as to priorities will, naturally, require careful consideration, consultation and planning.
The basic approach of the working document was outlined to the provincial ministers of health in February of this year. The provinces unanimously endorsed it and felt that it offered great opportunities for raising the health of Canadians.
The working document will be the subject of careful review and analysis with provincial governments in the months to come in a way analogous to the study of the Working Paper on Social Security in Canada. I have asked that the working document be included on the agenda of the federal-provincial meeting of deputy ministers in June and I am planning to discuss it with my provincial colleagues at our next meeting.
It is hoped that the working paper which has been in preparation for several months will help to develop a high level of general public awareness of its objectives and will generate informed discussion among all Canadians- individuals, groups, professions as well as governments.
This working document, therefore, is not limited in its scope only to matters where federal initiatives are needed. We hope it will not only appeal to all hon. members but to the general public as well. Most important, we offer it as a rallying point for all sectors of Canadian society who have a role to play in improving the physical and mental wellbeing of Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: AIR CANADA FREIGHT RATES
speechtext:
The management of Air Canada advises as follows: 1. The basic measure used by Air Canada for assessing freight rate is the weight of the shipment, with the resulting rate reflecting the distance involved. Depending upon the size of the shipment, a container rate, a specific rate for the commodity in question or general rate may be offered.
May 1, 1974

2.	Air Canada is a common carrier which means that rates apply equally to all consumers who meet the conditions applicable to the rate, i.e. shipment is the same commodity, shipment is the same weight, shipment is the same origin and destination.
3.	Price quotations are given in local currency or their dollar equivalent.
4.	The basic rate of exchange which applies is the IATA set of rates of exchange or the bankers' buying rate, whichever provides the greatest revenue.
5.	The freight rates are changed to reflect fluctuations in bank rates of exchange when the variance exceeds 2.5 per cent up or down.
6.	Rate changes are generally made on the basis of changes in costs of handling and carrying the traffic involved, or to fill aircraft space which under certain operational conditions is difficult to fully utilize.
Order Paper Questions
7.	General commodity rates are essentially the same to and from Canada. However, in order to correct directional traffic imbalances, a number of specific commodity rates are available which are directional in nature and generally result in lower levels from Canada compared with to Canada.

For what reason does the government not direct the Bank of Canada to sell its numismatic collection and remit to the government the money derived from the sale, in order that the government use the money to help the people survive the inflationary monetary policy of the Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: BANK OF CANADA-NUMISMATIC COLLECTION
speechtext:
1. No
attempt has been made to determine the current value of the Numismatic Collection of the Bank of Canada. A large part of the collection had been in the hands of the Federal Government for many years and was transferred to the Bank of Canada from the Public Archives of Canada in 1965. Other considerable portions have come to the Bank as gifts from public-spirited Canadian citizens and institutions. Part of the collection, predominantly Canadian numismatic items, has been acquired by purchases form private collectors and numismatic dealers in Canada and other countries during the past twelve years. Many of the items in the collection are unique and others are so rare as to almost never come on the public market. It would therefore be almost impossible to calculate a realistic market value for the collection.
2. Having the sole authority for the note issue the central bank has a natural interest in Canadian paper money and over its earlier years it gradually accumulated

May 1, 1974

a limited collection of numismatic materials related to this interest. Aware of this, finding no comparable interest or expertise elsewhere and deeming the development of a collection not to be part of its responsibility, the Public Archives, with the approval of the Secretary of State, in the mid '60's, turned over its substantial but unorganized volume of numismatic holdings to the Bank with a view to the establishment of a comprehensive representative numismatic collection. The Bank's collection, now regarded as the National Numismatic Collection, is an important part of Canada's heritage. Almost every political, social and economic event in our history is reflected in the coins, tokens and paper money which have been used in Canada during the past 300 years and plans are under way for a money museum in the Bank's new Head Office building project in which the Collection will be displayed for the benefit of the Canadian public.
3. It is considered to be in the public interest to have a national numismatic collection.

subsubtopic: MEMBERS FROM JOINING UNION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General. In view of the fact it is federal government policy to allow federal public servants to belong to a union or association of their choice, and in view of the fact that some members of the RCMP are showing an inclination toward forming some type of organization, will the minister give favourable consideration to amending the present legislation which prohibits the RCMP from this action so that these federal public servants can enjoy the same privileges as all others?

subsubtopic: MEMBERS FROM JOINING UNION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when parliament passed the Public Service Staff Relations Act in 1967 it deliberately excluded the RCMP as a group of employees from qualification for unionization under that act. In the last two years we have held meetings with representatives of the constables, corporals and sergeants of the RCMP in Ottawa for a week each year, and they have shown no interest in the formation of a union. We know there is an information meeting to be held by the police association in Vancouver tonight and there is to be another in Toronto tomorrow night. We shall be watching these meetings with interest.

subsubtopic: MEMBERS FROM JOINING UNION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MEMBERS FROM JOINING UNION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Well, I have been asked to send somebody from my office to the meeting in Toronto and I am doing so. As I say, the law now forbids the RCMP from forming a union. I personally believe it is not in the public interest that members of the RCMP should belong to a union, but we shall be watching the situation closely.

maintopic: POSSIBLE HARASSMENT OF MEMBERS INTERESTED IN FORMING UNION

maintopic: RIGHT OF MEMBERS TO ADVOCATE CHANGE IN LAW CONCERNING UNION MEMBERSHIP
speechtext: Even though the law as it now stands forbids the formation of unions among members of the RCMP, is there any reason why they should be denied freedom of speech to advocate a change in the law without, as a result, being penalized under the mounted police act?

maintopic: RIGHT OF MEMBERS TO ADVOCATE CHANGE IN LAW CONCERNING UNION MEMBERSHIP
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, they are not. I tried to convey to the House a few moments ago that in the last two years the men of the RCMP, the non-commissioned officers and the men, have freely elected representatives from each division in Canada and sent them to Ottawa to discuss their problems with the administration. I have personally met with them privately and I asked them this very question. They spoke to me very forcefully and articulately on many other subjects, but they told me at that time that of the 16 divisional representatives only one favoured a union. The other 15 did not.

maintopic: RIGHT OF MEMBERS TO ADVOCATE CHANGE IN LAW CONCERNING UNION MEMBERSHIP
speechtext: I should like an answer to the question I asked. The question is simply this: are the mounted police to be denied freedom to advocate changes in the law or are they to be subject to penalties for exercising that freedom which every Canadian has a right to exercise?

maintopic: RIGHT OF MEMBERS TO ADVOCATE CHANGE IN LAW CONCERNING UNION MEMBERSHIP
speechtext: No. No penalties will be imposed upon them for exercising their freedom of speech.

maintopic: RIGHT OF MEMBERS TO ADVOCATE CHANGE IN LAW CONCERNING UNION MEMBERSHIP
speechtext: With regard to those officers seeking some kind of alliance with the police association, or the formation of a union, can the minister advise us what he is prepared to do to deal with the underlying discontent within the force which prompts such action on the part of the RCMP?

maintopic: RIGHT OF MEMBERS TO ADVOCATE CHANGE IN LAW CONCERNING UNION MEMBERSHIP
speechtext: I have met with many groups within the RCMP. As a matter of fact, when I visit detachments I make a point of discussing matters with the men. I must say that on the whole there is no discontent; the morale is quite high. There have been problems among individuals and we are hoping to meet those problems. We are trying to implement many new methods of dealing with this question of morale, arrangements for consultation and so on with the men in the force. In the past year we have taken a number of measures to that effect.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to move second reading of Bill C-29, to amend the Combines Investigation Act in relation to profiteering practices. This bill will enable the government to temporarily freeze prices on
1938

May 1, 1974
Profiteering Practices
goods where there is evidence of profiteering and will provide a means to roll prices back in these circumstances. The bill reflects the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) commitment to Parliament and Canadians made last year when he said the government would be prepared to introduce measures to protect the consumer against those who may attempt to take advantage of the present situation by unwarranted price increases. The Prime Minister further stated during the throne speech debate in February that:
We will not allow corporate profiteers ... to pile up unearned windfall profits at the expense of the people of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the government has already applied a broad set of policies to attack inflation and reduce its effects on Canadians. Along with this, by introducing Bill C-29, the government is carrying out the commitment as expressed in the Speech from the Throne to stop business from taking advantage of current economic conditions to unduly enhance profits. The legislative proposals would stop, in specified circumstances, a producer or merchant from exacting, on the sale or distribution of an article, a profit margin greater than that customarily obtained. The bill would also stop attempts to enhance the price at which an article is eventually sold by withholding from sale or distribution an inventory of that article substantially in excess of that normally held. Such practices defined in the proposed legislation as exceptionable trade practices are generally regarded by Canadians as particularly unacceptable in inflationary conditions. These practices would become unlawful in the circumstances set out in the legislative proposal now before the House.
The bill proposes that the exceptionable trade practices provisions would come into force on declaration by the governor in council. Such declarations would be made by the governor in council normally after consideration of reports issued by the Food Prices Review Board or such other boards as might be established under the authority of the Inquiries Act or other legislation to inquire into the causes of particular price increases, actual or proposed.
Before making a declaration, the governor in council would have to be satisfied that a situation existed or was likely to exist which would have a substantial effect on the price of an article or a class of articles, thus tending to seriously affect the living costs of all or a great majority of Canadians. But in emergency cases, declarations could also be made by the governor in council without first having had a board report, where it was satisfied that such a situation existed and that immediate action was required to protect the public interest.
Declarations made under the proposed law would be specific, applying to a particular article or articles at all or any levels of distribution. The order giving effect to the declaration would specify the period of time during which the declaration was to be effective up to one year. However, the governor in council could extend the period of time initially specified for further periods of up to six months if satisfied that the situation giving rise to the declaration continued to exist. In making a declaration, the governor in council could also invoke the price notification provisions set out in the legislation. Under these

provisions suppliers could not increase the price of the article in question over its base price unless the director of the combines investigation branch was notified 30 days in advance of the proposed increase or such shorter period as may be specified by the governor in council.
The application of these provisions will have the effect of imposing a temporary freeze on the price of the articles in question during the notification period. The governor in council would prescribe by regulation the definition of the base price for the purpose of this notification procedure.
The definition of base price prescribed could vary in accordance with the article declared and the practices under which it is normally sold. For example, the base price might be the price charged on a certain date, or such higher price as the firm can demonstrate that it customarily charged during the preceding 30 days. The reason for this wording in this hypothetical example would be to avoid forcing firms who happened to be having a sale on a certain date to use the special sale price as the base price. It is important to note that the base price is prescribed only for pre-notification purposes and does not necessarily have a relationship to a customary profit margin.
Under the bill, the governor in council would also have authority to make exemptions from the pre-notification requirements. Depending on the circumstances, one would expect that for very small firms, for example, it would be possible to exempt them from pre-notification rules as such a procedure could impose an unreasonable and onerous requirement on such small firms. However, such an exemption would cover pre-notification requirements only and the price of the article or articles supplied by the exempted firm would still be required to meet the customary profit margin test.
The new measures would not apply to agricultural produce in an unprocessed state when owned or sold by the primary producer or to unprocessed fishery products when owned or sold by a fisherman. It could apply, however, at other levels of distribution for such products. The governor in council when making a declaration would issue guidelines specifying the manner in which suppliers would determine the profit margin that they customarily obtain and which they could not exceed.
Customary profit margin could be defined differently for each level of distribution. For example, the method to be applied could be different for a manufacturer as opposed to the retailer of a product. The term "customary" could be prescribed to the margin realized during a given past period of time. For example, the guidelines could stipulate-and this is only a hypothetical example-that the customary profit margin would be based on the average profit margin of three years in a specified five year period, which could exclude the immediately preceding year.
In setting out the manner of determination of customary profit margin, consideration would be given to the prevailing economic climate and the business cycle of the particular sector. In addition, the guidelines would be sufficiently flexible to take into account their application to firms operating at low levels of profit or at a loss, or to new businesses.
May 1, 1974

The administrative and investigative machinery required to administer the proposed legislation would be provided through the office of the director of investigation and research under the Combines Investigation Act. Immediate steps are being taken to provide additional resources for these new duties. To ensure administrative feasibility, the legislative proposal would broaden the powers of delegation of the director so that responsibility for administering the exceptionable trade practice provisions could be fully delegated to a deputy director. In conducting inquiries, the deputy director would exercise the same powers as those conferred on the director and the Part I of the Combines Investigation Act.
The director would be required by the legislation to conduct an inquiry where he had reason to believe that a supplier was engaging in or was about to engage in an exceptionable trade practice. Inquiries would also be initiated by the director when directed to do so by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Such inquiries could only be instituted, of course, where a declaration from the governor in council was in effect covering the category of article or supplier in question and would be a key step in the process of enforcing the revisions in the law and regulations against those not complying with them.
In determining whether to initiate an inquiry, the director under the act would have access to the information and research obtained by the original board of inquiry, if there was one, unless it had been collected on a confidential basis. Information on supply and prices normally collected by various departments and not otherwise confidential in the government would be available to him. He would also be able to evaluate and compare the information in the price notification notices of all firms supplying the article or articles covered by the declaration.

As I was saying, he would also be able to evaluate and compare price notification notices of all firms supplying the article or articles in question. It is expected that the public would also bring information to the attention of the director, which would assist him in deciding whether to carry out an inquiry or continue it if the information came in the course of one being carried out.
Once a declaration was made, firms would calculate their customary profit margins and their base prices in accordance with the guidelines established by the Governor in Council. If a firm found that it is within the profit margin guidelines, it would not be required to take any
Profiteering Practices
action until it wished to raise a price above the base price. Before giving notice to the Director of Investigation and Research, which would have to be done 30 days prior to the price increase, or such lesser time as is specified, it would have to ensure that the new price would not result in a profit margin in excess of that customarily obtained.
However, if the firm calculated its customary profit margin and found that it was exceeding the guidelines, it would be expected to roll back its price. Failure to prenotify a price increase after declaration with regard to the product covered by it, could result upon indictment in imprisonment for two years or, on summary conviction, to a fine not exceeding $10,000 or to imprisonment for one year or both.
The Restrictive Trade Practices Commission, reconstituted as the Trade Practices Commission, would hear complaints from the director about exceptionable trade practices; for example, that a person was selling or about to sell the article so as to obtain a profit margin greater than the one prescribed by the act and regulations. If on the basis of the application made by the director, the commission was satisfied that the person to whom the application related was engaging in or about to engage in such an "exceptionable trade practice", it could order the person to cease and desist from engaging in the practice. Such an order, in effect, would roll back that person's prices to the appropriate level to meet the customary profit margin requirements.
In addition, the commission could require the supplier to give up all or any portion of the excess revenues he had realized as a result of his engaging in the "exceptionable trade practice". The commission could require the supplier to give up this excess revenue in one of three ways: either by refunding it to the person from whom he derived the excess revenue or, if those persons were not reasonably identifiable, by an appropriate reduction in the sale price to persons thereafter acquiring the article from him or finally, if neither of the first two methods were practicable, by paying it to the Receiver General. The Governor in Council would also have the authority to vary or rescind any order of the commission.
Once a declaration was made, superior courts would be authorized under the legislation to issue interim injunctions at any time on application by the Attorney General of Canada enjoining suppliers from engaging in exceptionable trade practices with respect to declared products. These injunctions would preclude firms from taking action which may be unwarranted until the director had an opportunity to carry out an inquiry or for the commission to reach a decision on a matter. Non-compliance with such court orders could result in a fine or imprisonment.
Also, orders of the commission would be enforceable through the courts with non-compliance resulting in the imposition of fines or imprisonment. Persons found guilty of non-compliance would be liable, if convicted on indictment, to imprisonment for two years and on summary conviction, to a fine of up to $10,000 or to imprisonment for one year or to both. Commission orders would also be subject to review under section 28 of the Federal Court Act.

It can be seen, Mr. Speaker, that the legislation provides a mechanism which will permit the Governor in Council to act promptly once there is a report by a board of inquiry, such as the Food Prices Review Board. Boards of inqi 'ry could be set up in other areas as required with instructions to report within an appropriately short period of time. Furthermore, if necessary, the Governor in Council could declare the powers of this act in force without a board report on the basis of information available generally to it from normal government sources.
It is the government's intention, following enactment of this legislation, to proceed to establishment of other boards to inquire into pricing practices in certain areas that have a pervasive effect on the economy. I say this to answer those incorrect assertions made by some who have suggested that the government would be prepared to take action only with respect to the food area. In fact, the government would be ready, where necessary, to make use of the authority it is seeking in this bill as soon as it is finally approved by parliament and proclaimed in force. In any event, the existence of this legislation should act as a deterrent to those who might otherwise feel they can engage in profiteering with impunity.
In addition to the temporary freeze resulting from the declaration, an interim injunction could be obtained at any time to prevent the continuance of profiteering practices until the inquiry can be completed and the commission has dealt with the matter. This means that this legislation would have an immediate impact the moment a declaration is made.
Also, there would not be uncertainty after a declaration has been made. The declaration itself would specify the levels of distribution and the products to which it applies. In addition, specific guidelines for the determination of base price and customary profit margins will be provided by the Governor in Council. Therefore, any businessman affected would be able to determine when to give advance notice of a price increase to the director. He would also be able to determine whether he was exceeding customary profit margins and should therefore roll back his price.
Attempting to provide a single definition for customary profit margin in the bill would, I submit, not be practical nor could it be fair or effective. I say this because no single definition would always be correct for each and every sector of the economy. That is why we believe it is necessary that the Governor in Council have the authority to establish guidelines for determining a profit margin based on a determination of what is appropriate for the product and sector in question.
Mr. Speaker, we believe the measures in this bill have general support and approval among Canadians. They would provide an instrument not now available, to permit the government, on behalf of the people of Canada, to deal with pricing practices, which are particularly unacceptable during inflationary periods. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I urge this House to give prompt second reading of this bill and to enable it to become law at the earliest possible date in the interests of all the people of this country.

The minister said during his press conference that food prices are the principal objective of the bill. We have heard this before, in the Speech from the Throne opening this session and in the Speech from the Throne opening the session prior to this one, when there was talk of setting up a food prices committee.
What do we have at this time for dealing with food prices. We have the Food Prices Review Board. It has been in existence for just over one year and has been described by the Consumers Association of Canada as a useless, expensive appendage. What relief has the Food Prices Review Board brought the Canadian consumer.

speechtext: None.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we believe it is necessary to limit profit margins during periods of high inflation. We believe it is necessary to limit profit margins to a level which enables industry to earn a rate of return sufficient to encourage new capital investment but, at the same time, to prevent windfall profits or uneconomic returns inherent in periods of inflationary expectations and new competitive market situations. This is inherent in our prices and incomes policy which was placed before this House more than one year ago.
May 1, 1974

What will this bill achieve? The difference, of course, is that ours is a comprehensive program. We do not intend by our program to fix the price of individual articles, as this bill sets out to do, and this, I might add, is one of the basic weaknesses of this bill. It is clear that the government does not intend to use this legislation to deal with inflation. Obviously, this will amount to a selective control policy. That is what the bill sets out to do. It will enable the new and very powerful Trade Practices Commission to freeze and roll back prices of every product or class of products, if it is found that their suppliers are making more than the customary profit margins or have withdrawn this product from the market to raise prices. This amounts to nothing more nor less than a selective price control policy. We reject that.
It seems most irregular to me that there should be such a dichotomy between what the government says and what it does. For example, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), who is a former minister of finance, told this House on March 15, 1974, in his capacity as acting minister of finance, as recorded at page 570 of Hansard that:
... selective controls ... are bound to be arbitrary. They are bound to have a selective effect which may not be acceptable.
He went on to say:
Selective controls are likely to single out particular groups for government action, and to leave others untouched. That is fine in theory, but the trouble is that it leads the government into a general program because every group in the community wants someone else to be the target of government action.
It is worth continuing to read from this speech. The minister went on to say:
The second point is one of general application... It is the problem of anticipation... All of the people selling goods in the country would be inclined to say, 'Let us get our increases put into effect before the government takes these measures.'
I suggest that the Minister of Consumer Affairs would have done well if he had read the words of the Secretary of State for External Affairs before introducing this bill. On the occasion in question, the minister condemned the use of selective controls because of Canada's large dependence on foreign trade. He said:
One would be forced, from putting on selective price controls, into selective export controls.
I commend those words to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray).
The use of selective controls by this government is nothing new. We are all well aware of the government's bread and milk subsidy programs, two programs which by the end of March had cost Canadian taxpayers $120 million and $87 million respectively, but did nothing to hold down prices. The government announced on September 4 of last year that milk prices would remain at current levels for 12 months. Notwithstanding that statement, milk prices to consumers rose last month, despite the subsidy, by about four cents a quart. We are told by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) that we can expect further increases in milk prices. Bread prices also rose from two cents to four cents a loaf last March, despite the $1.25 per bushel wheat subsidy which was imposed on September 4 to hold down prices, and despite the unheeded mumblings and grumblings of the relatively impotent
Profiteering Practices
Food Prices Review Board. Of course, the crowning failure of selective controls by this government was in its attempt to control beef prices and increase production by introducing a beef subsidy last March 15. The result was a complete disruption of the cattle market and even heavier losses to cattle producers.
This is the kind of result selective controls have on producers and consumers. Yet this is the kind of control the government is opting for under this proposed legislation. I wonder when the government will finally wake up to the fact that selective controls are inherently unfair, in view of the fact that they tend to discriminate against certain sectors of Canadian society and certain products. Only a comprehensive price and income stabilization program could hold the line on inflation while not jeopardizing any particular group.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been referring to this bill as an anti-inflation measure. Really, a most careful scrutiny of the contents of the bill would cause even the most objective observer to harbour the gravest doubts about it. I doubt if this piece of legislation will do anything at all to combat inflation. If the government's past performance can be used as an indicator, it is easy to see that it has consistently refused to accept the recommendations of various agencies to hold down even the most blatant examples of price increases.
Consider the report of the Food Prices Review Board on eggs. This report was made by the board on January 9. At that time the board said that egg prices were too high, and it recommended that the government take steps immediately to roll back the price of eggs. The following day the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs said he would do something, that he would take action on the report. When the House resumed, the buck was passed by the minister, who is the best buck passer in the government-and God knows we have a cabinet of buck passers-to the Minister of Agriculture, who is no mean performer himself when it comes to buck passing. He, in turn, passed the buck to the Farm Products Marketing Council, where the buck has stopped. We have not heard from that body since then, notwithstanding the fact that eggs have risen in price over 31 per cent in 12 months in Canada, and no action has been taken to date. Surely the minister knows that eggs are a most important source of protein for low income earners of this country.
The situation with regard to rising bread prices was identical. The Food Prices Review Board stated that any increase beyond two cents a loaf would be unwarranted. The government refused to take any action and prices went up in some cases as much as four cents a loaf. With the labour unrest in the country and the difficulties of the small bakers, we can expect even greater increases in the price of bread this year. In light of this experience, it seems to be too pious a hope to expect the government to now change its stance and start accepting the recommendations of its various boards and agencies.
It is important to note that this bill merely gives the government the option of acting to prevent price increases. There are no built-in guarantees that the government will do so. Even if the Trade Practices Commission recom-

May 1, 1974
Profiteering Practices
mends a price roll-back or price freeze, cabinet may choose to ignore it. In view of so many past examples of just this kind of thing, we are really not expecting much from the government if this bill in fact ever becomes law.
As it stands, this bill seems to be a mere piece of fluff and unworkable in its present form. It gives all the appearance of being hastily contrived and a measure of political expediency.

speechtext: The determination of what are excess profits is so vague as to be almost meaningless. We had hoped the minister would enlighten us on that today.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: How could he when he doesn't know?

speechtext:
That is right. That is why we got no further enlightenment from him today.
Another point of vagueness in the bill is the determination of the base price of a commodity under examination. This is to be up to the discretion of the governor in council. In addition, the cost of a product is to be computed on a basis consistent with that used in the last completed fiscal period of the supplier. A determination of profit margins using these criteria could result in gross injustices, both to the producers and to consumers who have to pay the price. So much depends on how cabinet interprets the margin of profit that nobody will know where he stands.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, has this government really envisioned the possible implications of its definition of excess profits? According to one economist, it would require a very large group of well informed bureaucrats, each having a sound knowledge of a particular industry, article or product to be able to give proper advice to the government. God knows that bureaucracy is large enough under this government.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Surely, the minister knows that profits are a cyclical phenomena and that establishing a customary profit margin for a product based on the last decade may not be an easy task. In fact, it may be impossible.
If you base your measure of customary profit margin for a firm on last year's performance, for example, it would not be appropriate for every industry. Some were depressed while some were having a bumper year. Therefore, this government will only be increasing an already large bureaucracy, and God only knows what the result will be. The Food Prices Review Board is a good example. When the Food Prices Review Board was set up on May 28, 1973, its initial budget was $500,000 and its permanent staff numbered about 20. Since then its budget has quadrupled to the point where it is almost $2 million and its staff has more than doubled to 48. In addition, the Food Prices Review Board has entered into 29 contracts for 31 studies, thereby further increasing its bureaucracy.

Let us take a look at the power of this bill. The cabinet is given the ultimate decision as to what action to take with respect to demanding payment from suppliers or price roll backs and freezes under this bill. It may, on its own initiative, declare an emergency situation and refer the pricing policy of a particular supplier to the Trade Practices Commission.
Again on its own initiative, it may order the supplier to pay the Crown what it has decided are undue profits. In my view, that constitutes an arbitrary imposition of tax without reference to a ways and means motion of this House. I hope the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) will have an opportunity to say more about that later.
In order for the cabinet and/or the proposed Trade Practices Commission to exercise the discretionary powers under this bill, it will be necessary to closely monitor the market place. The minister may say that this role will be carried out by the Food Prices Review Board. I see the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen), a distinguished member of the food prices committee, smiling because he is skeptical. He knows whereof I speak. If we had to depend on the Food Prices Review Board to do the monitoring necessary under this bill, I would tell the House that this speaks for itself. Furthermore, the process by which this bill would become operative could be a long and cumbersome one which would considerably diminish its effectiveness.
Editorial writers and columnists all across the country have either dismissed the bill as so much political puffery, which it is, or have described it as bad law, which it is, that should never find its way as presented into the statute books of this country. The bill is imprecise in its application and vague in its definition. We have a responsibility to all our constituents. It would hang like a sword over every business person in the country because it could be selectively applied at any time. In the words of today's lead editorial in the Globe and Mail "There would be no fair warning". After the contribution by the minister today, he would do well to sit and ponder what he has produced before this House.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

Let me make it clear that this party utterly rejects the position that it should stay on the statute books of this country in its present form. If the opportunity presents itself, we will be moving amendments to try and strengthen and improve what is good about the bill and delete what is bad.
My point is that this bill is unacceptable to this party in its present form. We merely look upon it as another halfhearted attempt by this government to hang on to power, another half-hearted attempt to fill the shopping basket of the NDP in order to buy time while the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) keeps telling us the worst is yet to come.
May 1, 1974

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friends and I have given the bill now before us very careful study. Indeed, we gave it very anxious study to determine whether it is a measure which can really help Canadians, which can really reduce the heavy burden of the increasing cost of living under which Canadian families now labour.
I want to emphasize that this is the only test which should be applied to this bill: will it in fact be of value to Canadian families? The ingenious framework underlying this measure-and it is extremely ingenious, so ingenious that it is a maze rather than a process-can obscure the issue, but cannot help it. We have also studied, for reasons I shall explain in a few moments, statements made by government spokesmen with respect to this bill-statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and by the minister who introduced this legislation and who will carry the responsibility for its implementation.
In view of the nature of the bill, we wanted to find out what the intentions of the government as to the application of the bill when it becomes law are likely to be. Mr. Speaker, I want to tell you immediately that on the basis of the bill which we have studied and on the basis of the timid statements made by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray), statements which I shall outline during the next few minutes, we find it impossible in conscience to support this measure.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: So long over there, its been nice seeing you!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
I want to say to members of the Conservative Party on my right that they would be in the same boat if they were across the aisle, because if legislation is to bring effective results for the benefit of the people of Canada at this stage in our history it would be necessary for the government to possess the will and the courage to challenge and reduce the powers of the corporate market. Unless a parliament and unless a government has the will to challenge corporate power in this country, whatever is presented will inevitably be mere window dressing incapable of any effectiveness.
Mr. Speaker, I said we have paid particular attention to statements made on behalf of the government with respect to this bill. Why have we done so? We have done so because this bill, unlike many others, depends entirely-I repeat, it depends entirely-on the manner in which it is implemented by the government. I remind members of the House that the proclamation of the bill is of no effect. If this bill were passed today and proclaimed tomorrow, proclamation would have not the slightest effect. None of the bill applies to anything when it is made law. This is literally the case. None of the bill applies to anything, because before it can make any impact a second step is required-a declaration, as the bill calls it, a declaration by the government making the provisions of the bill applicable to an article or class of articles. The government
Profiteering Practices
can either declare the entire bill applicable or they can declare only part of the bill to be applicable; they are not obliged to declare sections 51, 52 and 53 which deal with a price freeze and with notification. They are not obliged to declare those sections if they do not wish to do so.
The bill gives the government a further power, the power to define what is meant by customary profits. This definition is binding on the director of research, binding on the commission, and, presumably, binding on the courts, if an issue gets to the courts. The government is the body which makes the decision as to what is the base price under sections 51, 52 and 53. It is the government which has the power to apply or not to apply the terms of the bill to an article. It has the power to apply the whole bill or to apply only part of it. It has the power to define customary profit, the power to define what is the base price. I say the bill is not worth the paper it is written on unless the government is prepared to take action. In these circumstances, the intention of the government-what the Prime Minister said when he told us the bill would be introduced, and what the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs said when he introduced the bill and made statements to the press outside this chamber-are of great importance in considering whether or not we can support this legislation, since they indicate what the intentions of the government are.
I turn, therefore, to a report in the Montreal Star of April 25, a report which appeared in a number of other papers. Here is part of this report. I quote:
The Prime Minister indicated that the legislation might not be proclaimed until needed. He suggested that the threat of it would be enough to stop companies from profiteering.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has been making these threats for months. I have not noticed that profiteering has stopped, and to suggest that this might happen is sheer silliness.
Then, I note what the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs said, according to a recent report. Again, I quote:
The minister indicated, however, that the powers were to be used sparingly. "They would only apply to the most serious and obvious cases".
So those are the intentions of the government. They bring down a bill which gives them the power to act and they inform the people of Canada that they do not intend to act, except, possibly, in the most serious and obvious cases. In other words, a little profiteering is okay, you can get away with it; only when there is immense profiteering on a scale that even the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) cannot deny, will the government act. And the Prime Minister says: Maybe we shall not have to act at all.
When the government tells us they are concerned about profiteering I cannot help recalling that both the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) have been going about the country in the last little while telling everybody within earshot and everybody who can read that profits and high profits are a good thing because they encourage investment and create jobs. Am I supposed to believe that a government consisting of the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, who made the statement to

May 1, 1974
Profiteering Practices
which I referred a few months ago, is likely to make this bill work except in cases no one could possibly overlook?
In fact, in one of the supporting documents the minister issued when he introduced the bill-and listen to this, Mr. Speaker; how can the minister expect us to support the measure in these circumstances-the statement appeared: "Available evidence does not suggest widespread abuses".
I do not know what the minister means by the word "abuses". All I know is that a report in the newspaper this morning of a private survey of 111 companies in this country showed an increase in corporate profits for the first quarter of this year amounting to 70 per cent over the first quarter of last year. Part of that increase was undoubtedly connected with exports going outside this country but a major portion was made out of the hide of the Canadian consumer. What more evidence does the minister require in order to show that there had been abuses?
We have placed on record on a number of occasions in this parliament the profits made by various sectors of the economy including, for example, figures showing that the profits made by Westons had risen 86 per cent in 1973. When the minister gave us an example in one of the documents he presented-I know he changed it today-he said the customary profit would be the profit made a year ago. That is not going to make George Weston cry or tremble in his boots. He is going to laugh all the way to the bank with that kind of active profiteering. I emphasize again my reference to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs as that is of particular relevance and particular emphasis because of the fact that under the act he is to administer this bill; he is to implement the bill. If this government continues and the job is left in his hands, in view of the statement he has made, that alone is reason enough for voting against this bill.
Members of my party and I have frequently emphasized that we are opposed to over-all price and income freezes and controls. I could not help but feel a little amused when the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) was castigating the government for the relatively small bureaucracy the bill might produce, and when he was suggesting a comprehensive price and income freeze and control. Really he ought to have had his tongue in his cheek, as I cannot think of anything that would require a larger bureaucracy, than that kind of policy.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: It would help the unemployment problem.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
We have opposed this and so have members of the Conservative party in spite of what they say. At one moment they say they want comprehensive price and income controls. At the next moment they say there will be no price control at the farm gate, and that is a pretty good exclusion. At the next moment somebody says that, of course we cannot freeze all wages and we will have to let somebody have a little more flexibility, and at the next moment somebody mentions some other exclusion. The reason they make these exclusions one after the other is that even they realize when they state it that their policy

is either unworkable or unjust, and is most likely both unworkable and unjust.
There are a lot of people who claim that certain workers in Canada should be prevented by law from striking. We have had evidence of the fact that because there is a law that makes striking illegal does not necessarily mean some people will not in the tragedy they find themselves, and in the distress from which they suffer, take action which may be unlawful as far as the law is concerned. To suggest that those people should have their wages frozen, that the hospital workers in Ontario should have their wages frozen for even 90 days, and for another year and a half or two years, is really too uncivilized.
We have equally rejected the idea that the government can do nothing, because there are areas in which action is possible. We have suggested among other things four ways in which to ease the pressure of inflation in Canada, and I have chosen my words carefully. I do not think any policy can, in the present international situation, remove the pressure of prices, and anybody who suggests that he can wave a wand and end inflation in Canada completely, does not know anything about economics, or is dishonest, or is both lacking in knowledge and dishonest. It cannot be done.
There are ways in which the burden of the cost of living can be reduced and there are ways in which profiteering at the expense of the people can be effectively stopped. We have suggested an effective agency with power to roll back unjustifiable increases in prices. We have urged an excess profits tax and we have urged a two-price system for a number of major commodities so that Canadians are not forced to pay the price for their own products that the international markets can now command. We have also urged on the government and on the country a policy on mortgages that would reduce mortgage rates to 6 per cent, which would be of immediate assistance to every family seeking a house and to every family renting a unit.
Of course, I appreciate that this bill does accept the idea that there is profiteering and that profiteering should be stopped, but I have no illusions about the fact that it was intended at least in part, before anybody on the Liberal side jumps to his feet, and I would even be inclined to suggest in major part, and even go further than that and suggest a significantly major part, as a sop to the NDP members in this House. But we do not intend to accept a piece of legislation that plays a hoax on the people of Canada.
Let me now deal with the bill itself. Why do I say it is a hoax? First, please note that it does not cover services, and that plays an important part in people's lives, because what is involved in services are not merely lawyers, doctors, engineers and architects, important as they are, but also involves banks, insurance companies, loan sharks, mortgage corporations, restaurants and transportation, although transportation has its own CTC, and all of these areas affect the cost of living directly. I simply do not know what kind of timidity prevents the bill from applying on a selective basis in all the areas that affect the living of Canadian people.
May 1, 1974

The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in more than one newspaper report I have read is quoted as having said that this bill does not apply to housing. If that is true, that alone condemns the bill as worthless.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Just imagine pretending to deal with profiteering and leaving the builders and developers to do as they like with the Canadian people and the lives of Canadian families. That is my first objection, that it does not apply to services, housing and that kind of area. Second, the minister has made clear in introducing the bill that the sections which give the government authority to invoke the provisions of the bill on its own without a prior inquiry would be used only in emergency cases. Those are his words.
In an emergency the government could itself without any prior inquiry declare the application of the bill to an article or class of articles. In order to do that the government would have to have some information. If it is to rely on information from the Department of Finance, from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce or Statistics Canada, if that is to be sufficient to deal with the situation, why in heaven's name do we have all this rigamarole about people making inquiries under the Public Inquiries Act? I ask the minister whom he is trying to fool. If it is possible to act on the basis of information already available through the normal departments of government, why is there this rigamarole in respect of this bill? The fact is that it is impossible for the government to act really on the kind of information that is available through the various departments. Therefore, I come to a very major omission in this bill which makes it exceedingly weak if not worse; that is, it does not provide for a continuing agency monitoring and inquiring into prices right across the line in this country.
If one meant business, if one were serious about this, obviously what one would do is have a continuing monitoring agency to see what is happening in respect of prices with the power either under the Public Inquiries Act or special powers, I do not care which, to look at the books of the companies enterprises and concerns involved so that there would be on a continuing basis the kind of information on which a government might quickly act. But we do not have that. We have no monitoring device which has any power. The government is to act on some information undefined at some time, God knows when. That is a big hole in the legislation.
I object as strongly as I can, thirdly, to the fact that the bill is given into the hands of a part-time commission. I just cannot understand that. I cannot understand it because it indicates to me a lack of seriousness. The job of implementing or administering this bill is given to the Trade Practices Commission as it is now to be called, the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission as formerly called, which has an immense job now under the old act. The new competition bill will add tremendously to its duties. It will be very busy dealing with all sorts of things that are now described and defined in the old act and in the new competition bill. We therefore ask whether giving that commission the job of looking after the cost of living
Profiteering Practices
of the Canadian people makes any sense to anyone who is serious about the matter.
The government realized what it was doing and in part tried to put somewhere in the bill a clause which says that any application by the director of research to the commission should be given priority insofar as is practicable. Insofar as it is practicable-who is to decide that and when? I suggest it is a sign of a lack of seriousness that the government could not establish a special commission full time that would be allocated to this important job, to this most important job so far as the lives of the Canadian people are concerned. If the government wished to make this a permanent commission, why does it not have a second chairman so that there would be a separate panel of the commission to deal with nothing else but the application and implementation of this legislation. It is my feeling that the absence of a full-time commission to deal with this simply fails to show seriousness.
Then, when we look at the way in which the information is to be gathered, again I cannot understand that. I may be missing something, but I studied the bill for two days. I have re-read it thoroughly until I know it almost by heart, and I just cannot see it. What is the normal process? Remember that the minister said that only in an emergency would the government act on its own motion. The normal process is an inquiry by someone under the Public Inquiries Act, either the Food Prices Review Board or the other inquiry that the minister said the government comtemplates appointing. So, you have one inquiry and on the basis of a report from that inquiry the government makes a declaration applying the act to certain articles. When it has done that there is another inquiry by the director of research and investigation of the Trade Practices Commission and when he has finished there is a third inquiry by the commission itself.
By the time this elongated process ends the skin of thousands of consumers will have been completely taken off.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
I have asked myself a dozen times since I read the bill, if these people mean business why is there this elongated complicated process. You appoint someone to make the inquiry and on the basis, of that inquiry you make a declaration and shoot it to the commission to make the order. If the commission feels it is necessary to have a hearing the parties concerned will have their day in court. This I fully support because it is part of our law and tradition. I have no objection to that. The commission has that hearing by appointing an inquiry before the declaration and after the declaration and then that is followed by a further inquiry by the commission. At every stage there is delay because of the way in which a company could withhold its books, lose its invoices or lose its bills and the way in which it can obfuscate and obscure the facts from the inquiry. The delay at every stage of the process makes this bill not a serious bill.
Then, we have an important part of the bill, clauses 51, 52 and 53, which contains the germ of what we in the New Democratic Party have been after for a couple or more years; that is the power to stop a price increase if it is undesirable and anti-social. Heaven's above, the steel cor-

porations have increased steel prices half a dozen times in the last 12 months, and steel enters into the construction of homes and of every appliance we use. The nickel manufacturers have increased the price of nickel. The prices of copper, lumber, bricks, cement have all increased. All of these things that enter into the cost of living have been increased immensely in the past 12 months. subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROFITEERING PRACTICES AND PERMANENT AND TEMPORARY MEMBERSHIP OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
When a thorough but quick inquiry is made and a price increase is found to be unjustified, there must be immediate authority to tell the company that they cannot increase their price. I invite members of this House, members of the press and the public to read sections 51, 52 and 53 carefully. What you will find is, first, as I have already said, that the government does not have to declare those sections; it can declare the rest of the act without them. Second, you will find that even when they declare those sections, all that will happen will be that the firm will have to give notice within 30 days or an earlier period. There is nothing in those sections that gives anybody except the court the authority to say to the firms: the price increase you propose is unjustified and you cannot have it.
Neither the commission nor the government is given the power to do that. So, in order to freeze the price after notification of a price increase, the minister was bold enough to say that he had the power to freeze the price. I tell him he is talking through his hat. He does not have that power. In order to freeze the price, the attorney general of Canada (Mr. Lang) will have to go to court and make an application for an interim injunction, which he could get ex parte under certain conditions.
I have practised enough law, not for very many years of my life but enough of it, to know that when you start on that road, the consumer will not get any help. There is a hearing in court and probably an appeal from the decision of the court, and God knows when the price freeze will actually apply. Why is that? If the government provides in the bill a way in which people must give notification of a price increase, then what is it that prevented this government, other than its lack of seriousness, from adding a subsection saying that in such cases the cabinet, the governor in council or the commission will have the authority to say; You cannot increase your price unless we give you permission to do so.

speechtext:
It does not say anything of the sort. Let the minister read his own bill. In order to get that, he will have to go to court.
The kernel of the bill, of course, is the definition of customary profit and the definition of base price. Why did the government make reference to what they call "customary profit"? This is where I think my friend, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), is wrong when he says that this bill represents selective price control. It is nothing of the sort. It is an ill-digested attempt to stop

some obvious, serious and visible profiteering, and that is all. If it were going to be a selective price control bill with any meaning, then I suggest that the criterion should have been a reasonable price in the light of increased costs of production, taking into account inflationary influences on the cost of production. An assurance should have been given to the consumers in Canada that the profits which have been made in the last two years at their expense will not be the guide as to what they are to pay after some law comes into effect, but the guide will be the price they paid before inflation became unbearable to the people of Canada, say two or three years ago, adjusted to the increased costs of production 'ncluding the weight of inflationary influences.
That is not a complicated concept and it could have been written into the law so that everybody would know, not only the consumer but the supplier, exactly what it is we are after, and no selective price control mechanism is of value if the price is held at the level which it has already reached in relation to the profits that the corporations have already made. For heaven's sake, how much more are you going to let the corporations make at the expense of the people of Canada?
I want to express one more criticism of the bill and then make a few more general comments before my time expires. I object to the fact that the bill says that inquiries are to be in private and that even the commission may, if it decides, hold its inquiries in private. One of the values of this kind of legislation is that the people of Canada know what is happening to them.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

Once the cabinet makes the decision that there is enough reason to declare the act applicable to certain suppliers and certain products, there is no excuse for having the inquiry in private, other than the protection of the profiteers.
Over a year ago we urged parliament and the government to establish a Food Prices Review Board with power. We got a Food Prices Review Board without power, and all the time that very intelligent chairman of the board goes around the country babbling things, the prices continue to go up. We agreed to the foreign investment bill, and after urging that it be strengthened we succeeded in having it strengthened, but so far only a part of it has been proclaimed. The most important part has not even been proclaimed, and I do not know what has happened to it. With regard to the Trade Practices Commission, let us remember the years that that commission has taken to deal with anything concerning the Canadian people. Let me remind you of the sugar cartel in Canada. After the three firms involved had already been fined, it took the commission ten more years before they got them into court again, and in the meantime there have been absolutely criminal increases in the price of sugar to the Canadian consumer, while the commission took ten years to find out again what it had found out ten years earlier.
I state to the government, to my friends in the House in all sections through you, Mr. Speaker, that we are not prepared to accept the kind of sop that the Food Prices Review Board has turned out to be.

The points which I made with regard to the bill, the statements of the government to which I referred, indicate clearly that neither the bill nor the government are serious about assisting the Canadian consumer in a meaningful and effective way. It is a sop to us which we are not accepting. It is a piece of political windowdressing that attempts to tell the Canadian consumer that something is being done for him when in fact nothing is being done for him.
Finally, we reached a decision, not with any glee because the condition of the Canadian people in the present situation deserves the attention of this parliament and of this government. Canadians deserve legislation that will reduce the burden of the cost of living on the Canadian family, that will really hold prices in selective areas at a reasonable level, and that will really hit everybody who is trying to profiteer at the expense of the Canadian consumer. We need such legislation, but we need legislation that is good, that is tough, that is effective, that is serious and that is meaningful. We cannot let the government get away with the kind of legislation it has now proposed, mere gestures in an area which is too serious to be treated with the contempt that, in my view, this bill suggests.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again we find that this government is not interested in solving problems. In an article published in La Presse the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) is reported as saying that this bill is first and above all intended as an instrument in the fight against inflation. Going through the bill clause by clause we realize that it will not solve inflation problems but change the name of the "Restrictive Trade Practices Commission" to the "Trade Practices Commission." It is fantastic to see how a name change can help people!
Furthermore, the number of standing members will be increased from 4 to 7. That might at least help create three more jobs but what will people derive from it? Absolutely nothing, probably a little less money. Three jobs will be created at the expense of the people of this country who will have to pay further taxes to pay for those three jobs. People did not benefit from it yet.
What about the authority to appoint five temporary members if necessary. The bill indicates further that that will not be used often.
Third, the commission has no other power than to inquire and report its findings to the minister but not on its own only after securing leave to inquire. They cannot even inquire on their own. They have to secure permission to inquire from the government. And there is still talk about wanting to solve inflation problems, those of the years 1980 or 1985 and not those of today. But when permission has to be secured to do a rush job type of inquiry as witnessed in recent years I am sure that people will feel the taste of inflation problems for a hell of a long time yet.
Fourth, the Governor in Council determines what products will be investigated. It seems to me this bill would allow for pressure to be applied on companies.
Profiteering Practices
Go and see them before the election with the bill and tell them: If you do not contribute to the election fund, your production will be declared under the legislation. If you contribute, we will let you go. The Liberal party is sticking a knife in the manufacturers. No provision of that bill deals with sectors which precisely contribute to inflation in Canada. Service industries, banks, finance companies and real estate operations are left out. Recently, the Bank of Canada was allowed to increase its interest rates. Now automatically, the chartered banks increased theirs, thus raising production costs in Canada. The government is not considering a review of that practice. If it prevented the banks from exaggerating, prices could be reduced and the public would be satisfied instead of leaving the so-called inflation die out, as it is now, but nothing is done.
Finally, the bill states that if there are abuses-after three series of inquiries, as was suggested by the hon. member who spoke before me-if the government decides that abuses actually took place it can force the manufacturer or the company to pay back the excess profit not to the consumer but to the government. This is a new method of taxation. They do not have the guts to go and tax people because it is not politically advisable but they found a new way of levying a new tax through companies. And who is going to foot the bill? Still good old John Q. Public because of shameless gouging not abusive practice on the part of companies but intellectually abusive practice on the part of this government. There is no proposed solution, nothing specific in the sense of facing any or all sectors of the economy with the possibility of consumer protection. The bill says only that if a government feels it should apply the act at some point it will do so but if it does not feel it should at some other point it will apply it in part or not at all. In other words, as was so properly suggested in the heading of a column by an economic critic, "An act that will check absolutely nothing." A non-act. We waste our time discussing pious wishes, leading Canadians to think they will be able to meet all their needs with their current purchasing power. If but a ray of hope could allow them to look forward to that then we could say an effort was made to help them. But Bill C-29 now before us indicates in no way any possibility or ray of hope for Canadians that their current purchasing power will enable them to meet all their needs. As I said earlier, banks and finance companies are allowed to increase their interest rates. There is complaining about higher salaries but the cost of production and production financing is allowed to go up to such an extent that no increase in salaries will ever catch up with production cost. In other words, the government cannot give any guarantee whatsoever, it is not seeking any means to ensure that $1 in wages will equal $1 in production. The situation is allowed to deteriorate and when we compare the figures with those of 1940, we realize that today $1 does not buy $1 in production, but 18 cents. There are loud complaints about inflation, international inflationary pressures, while in our countries, the cost of houses is allowed to get higher. For instance, we still have an 11 per cent tax on building materials that is another factor in price hikes. Nonetheless, we complain about inflation!
Legislation like Bill C-29 is introduced, a bill which is not really a bill, but simply a sheet of paper to make the

These, Mr. Speaker, were the few comments that I wished to make and, in closing, I should like to tell the minister that he should not only try to put the population to sleep but to wake up himself and as soon as possible, because it is not with a bill like this one that he will stop the inflationary price increase and the arrogance of certain companies like the oil product companies, for instance, or the sugar manufacturers, who, as was stated a while ago, could not care less about the government and continue to increase their prices. But the government is not at all serious in introducing such a bill, and I hope that the minister will at least have the decency to wake up before third reading and propose amendments to the House or accept amendments which will at last enable the population to have if not a satisfactory legislation, at least a partly logical one instead of a nonsensical one.
