Mr. Speaker, I believe that, once again, the government has introduced a good bill because one hears from the other side of the House speeches of contradictory indignation. The NDP contends that this bill would tie the hands of business and inhibit its ability to compete in world markets, an ability which is important as we are an exporting nation. Presumably the NDP is thinking of the way business should be run under an NDP government. I suggest that under such a government, unemployment would rise to over 20 per cent, and that government would be kicked out, as well it should be. I am referring to the tying-of-the-hands-behind-the-back of business approach of the NDP.
On the other side of the record, we hear the contradictory indignation of the Conservative party. What does the leader of the party suggest we should do with regard to those exorbitant or unconscionable profits being made by a very small segment of our business community. We should, as the Progressive Conservative party suggested in British Columbia, hold an informal inquiry. This bill occupies ground somewhere in between those two positions. We say that in cases where business is making an unconscionably large profit the government is obliged to act. That is the philosophy behind the bill.
I was surprised to hear the leader of the NDP this afternoon say that he could not understand why inquiries in relation to excess profits should be conducted in private. I think he has been a politician too long, and too far removed from the courts and the days when he was a practising lawyer. He stated that if there were some

suggestion of some particular business making unconscionable profits, that business should be deemed to be guilty and be required to prove its innocence in the full glare of publicity. I suggest, with respect, that is contrary to everything we have been taught under the British system of justice. The hon. member, after the next election, will be given the opportunity to return to the practice of law and learn what justice under our constitution means.

speechtext:
We also heard members say that the government has done nothing to fight inflation in Canada. We can take that to be nothing but political rhetoric, because when such people are faced either this year or next, with a list of the things the government has done, they will be forced to admit it has done a tremendous amount to combat inflation.
What does this bill endeavour to do. As was indicated in the Speech from the Throne and in speeches of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) before and since that time, the government has been actively exploring the means to prevent profiteering from increasing prices. As a result, we have the bill before us to amend the Combines Investigation Act in relation to profiteering practices. It will provide the government with authority to protect Canadians from certain price gouging and profiteering practices which can occur in present conditions of inflation. I submit the government is carrying out its responsibility in this area because it is concerned that certain business enterprises have been taking advantage of current economic conditions and unduly enhancing their profits.
The available evidence does not suggest that these abuses are widespread, but if one listens to the political rhetoric of the opposition one might think that they are extensive. I submit that the proposed measure will enable the government to deal with these abuses where they are found to exist. No such legislation now exists, and the government is obliged to bring forward a measure such as this. This is not the only measure, but is one of the measures in this area.
In my view, this bill will be a boon to those businesses making large but not excessive profits, because they will be given the opportunity to put before the commission or tribunal facts and figures to show that their profits are not exorbitant. They will be able to deal with political rhetoric as practised by the NDP, and the NDP will learn that you cannot fool all the people all the time, a message they have been slow to learn.
Recently, the position adopted by the NDP with regard to percentages was attacked by the Ottawa Journal, which showed how ridiculous is the approach of that party when it considers increased profits in percentage terms. That newspaper mentioned a mining enterprise which had lost substantial sums of money for 10 years and in one year, according to the criterion of the NDP, had increased its profits by 4,000 per cent. It asked, would this increase in profits be challenged as exorbitantly large in view of the losses sustained over the last 10 or 15 years.
It is interesting to note that when we deal with small amounts of money, or small increases in profits, percent-
May 1, 1974

ages are quoted. When we speak of return on investment, and there is a minimum return on investment, we hear millions of dollars mentioned, not percentages.
The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) indicated that the Special Committee on Trends in Food Prices met several times and made excellent recommendations, most of which the government accepted. Probably only one has not been accepted, the recommendation with regard to establishing the standing committee on consumer affairs. I bring that recommendation to the minister's attention. It was an excellent one.
It was suggested that the Food Prices Review Board is a monitoring board. The food prices committee did not reach its decision lightly. Our terms of reference said that we had to confine our recommendations to the food industry. It was a Progressive Conservative government of Alberta which recommended that it not be a tribunal with powers to roll back or fix prices. Their recommendation was a monitoring board. In effect, that recommendation came also from other sources. It was solely the decision of the food prices committee. It was the decision of the committee based upon evidence presented to it by no less an authority than the Progressive Conservative government of Alberta. This Food Prices Review Board came up with excellent reports. I am not surprised that it is being attacked by the Progressive Conservative party because it showed the temporary wage and price controls policy of the Conservatives for the sham it is.
In times of shortage, we bring in this kind of legislation to cope with someone who might gouge as a result of the inflation which exists today in Canada. However, in times of shortage you do not put on controls. You do not try to control the import of foodstuffs from outside the country. The Conservatives have yet to indicate how they would control prices established in the international market.
A careful reading of the report of the Special Committee on Trends and Food Prices will indicate that among the recommendations there is a suggestion that one of the causes of inflation, particularly in the food industry which probably has the greatest impact, is the effect of increasing production. It is spelled out throughout the Speech from the Throne that this, in fact, is an area in which we must be moving. We must increase production, not only on the farms, but in the manufacturing industry. That is the approach that will win in the long run, not some temporary panacea such as wage and price controls.
The political speeches we heard this afternoon were almost a gasp of desperation from the opposition. It is interesting that one member says there is no place for a westerner in the Progressive Conservative party. On the other hand, we find that in Quebec there is a place in the Conservative party for a candidate judged to be too separatist by the Union Nationale party.

Mr. Speaker, I would be happy to do so. Apparently the hon. member was not listening to all my speech. He only listened to a part of it. I indicated that the
Profiteering Practices
official opposition party, in its attack on this bill, was not making a sincere attack. It is really a desperation measure brought on by the splits within that party. The are not attacking the bill on its merits, but are simply trying to nudge their new-found NDP friends into an election.
No one suggests that this bill is the complete answer to the problem of inflation and rising prices. It is simply an attempt to attack one area where individuals might be taking advantage of the present situation. It is wrong to suggest no other measures have been taken. I could just list a few things. We have lowered income tax, particularly for those at the lower end of our tax scale. We increased family allowances, old age security, the guaranteed income supplement, veterans pensions and the Canada Pension. This is only one more measure in the attack we are making within the scope of an individual country to fight inflation.
If this bill and the other steps I have suggested are not the answer, we have to look to other parties for alternatives. What would be the situation if the official opposition had been the government for the past 16 months? We certainly would not have had a bill like this, although most assuredly we would have needed it. That party was advocating a deficit of $2 billion to $5 billion. It has not made up its mind how far it should go. What would that have done to inflation in this country? We are a trading country. That measure would have induced inflation.
The official opposition has talked of a 90 to 120 dav freeze. When criticized, they decided it would not work too well and opted for 90 days until my colleague, the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher) pointed out that if you interfere in the market place to this extent, you cannot do it on a temporary basis. He said that price increases and production would simply be held back, and we would be hit with their full effect at the end of the 90 or 120 day period. We heard suggestions from time to time that the measure that should be taken would be to put on wage and price controls for a period of two years. I must say that 33 per cent of the young Conservatives had the good sense to realize this was not the policy to combat inflation, particularly the kind we have in Canada today.
We hear the opposition parties talking about the fact that interest rates have been on the increase and should be lowered. They say that money should be lent at lower rates. Who would lend? When I hear that, it reminds me of the story that has been told in this House about the lady who went to a store and told the storekeeper she could buy bananas down the road for 20 per cent less. When the chap asked why she did not go down the road to buy bananas for 20 per cent less, she said they did not have any. The storekeeper told her that when he did not have any bananas, his price was 50 per cent less. That seems to be the philosophy of the opposition party.

country or any political party to face, we spelled out the problem in the throne speech. We indicated the measures to be taken. Just as important, we indicated some of the measures not to be taken; certainly not the imposition of wage and price controls.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many Canadians are asking why the government had the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) bring in this bill as an amendment to the Combines Investigation Act. I suppose some might suggest that this measure is given an aura of respectability in the sense it is not a new act, but an amendment to a long-standing and existing act. It may gain some respectability by appending these new powers to an existing tribunal, the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission, which will now become known as the Trade Practices Commission.
There is another explanation that may have more credibility and which is receiving a much wider degree of acceptance in Canada. It is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), who might normally be expected to introduce a legislative measure of this nature, wanted to get as far away from this piece of legislation as possible. Indeed, I think that the presence or lack of presence of ministers in the House this afternoon is a clear indication that the government has some reservations about this legislation. They have thrown it out as a trial balloon. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) called it a sop to his party. The government has made a scapegoat of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs because it now appears he will fall flat on his face.
The other significant aspect of this debate is a statement made today by the leader of the New Democratic Party. I do not have the advantage of the Hansard record of today's proceedings, but I will quote the statement as accurately as I can. I think it is important, not only in the sense that it tells a story concerning this piece of legislation and the evolution of the NDP, but because it tells the story of this 29th parliament and what has been going on, if the people of Canada do not already know. The leader of the NDP said "We are not prepared to accept again the sort of sop that the Food Prices Review Board turned out to be". To my way of thinking, that is a candid admission that they have been handed sops in the past. They have accepted them, they have been had, and the people of Canada now know that. I do not really want to gloat and say "We told you so" but maybe this is the importance of the conversion we have witnessed today. It is a sign that a minority party in this House, a party which has for so many months prevented the people of Canada from having a say con-

cerning the economic questions confronting this nation, has at last admitted that it is time for a change.
The leader of the NDP attached a good deal of importance to statements made by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs since this bill was given first reading on Monday. He also referred to statements made by the Prime Minister. Since the powers for which provision is made in the bill are powers which are delegated to the executive, and to a tribunal, and since they do not become operative automatically, but at the pleasure of the government, the hon. member for York South was correct in saying it was important to take these statements into account when assessing what the government will likely do following the bill's enactment. That is a responsible position and it is one which members of my party will take.
I am glad to see the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in his place because I want to throw out some challenges to him. Perhaps he can arrange for some answers to be provided. Can the minister indicate who are the suspected offenders in terms of gouging and profiteering? What are the mischiefs to which the legislation is directed? Is it the price of oil, is it the oil companies which the government intends to reach through this legislation?
Now, if we look at the bill carefully we find that oil may be exempt. The bill refers constantly to "articles", and the term, "article" is defined in the present Combines Investigation Act as meaning "an article or commodity which may be the subject of trade or commerce". Mr. Speaker, there is another bill before parliament, presently in committee, Bill C-7, an Act to amend the Combines Investigation Act, which extends the definition of "article" and included in that extended definition is "energy, however, generated". We can only conclude that if the government found it necessary in Bill C-7 to extend the definition of "article" and if the bill now before us were to receive speedy passage before Bill C-7, and we had to rely on the old definition of "article", then "energy, however generated" would be excluded.
Let me suggest some further examples. Does the government have in mind the price of eggs? The price of eggs may be exempt under this legislation because it relates to an agricultural product. There may be profiteering on the part of those who sell eggs, but they are exempt. What else does the minister have in mind? He has declined to give us any of the necessary information. The whole philosophy of this legislation, if there is any, is to place these powers in the hands of the Governor in Council, the cabinet, which in turn may seek the advice of the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission. Trust us, they say, and somewhere along the line we may take action. In my view, this is not good enough. It is too arbitrary. It runs contrary to a fundamental rule of law, a fundamental principle which should be contained in all legislation which receives the approval of the House.
Consider certain other sections of this legislation. What about services? Services were mentioned by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and by the hon. member for York South. Now the minister certainly mentioned them when he spoke not long ago in the debate on
May 1, 1974

Bill C-7. They are included in that bill. He said that 20 per cent of the gross domestic product of this country was comprised of services, and that this percentage figure was increasing. Yet for some mysterious reason which the minister could have explained in the last two days, services are not included. Is the minister suggesting that there is no possibility of profiteering or gouging on the part of the professions in Canada? Is he suggesting that management consultants, accountants, those involved in private transportation enterprises, advertising agencies and consumer finance companies are incapable of engaging in profiteering or gouging? Why were they excluded? Again, this is a selective policy, and it is one which should not be supported by members of this House.
Reference has been made to the cost of housing. Again, I refer to the definition of "article" as contained in the Combines Investigation Act. If this bill were to be dealt with expeditiously and passed quickly-I hope it will not-the word "article" which would be applicable would not include housing. There is a new definition of article in Bill C-7 which may include aspects of housing. I quote: "article" ... includes:
(b)	deeds and instruments relating to or evidencing the title or right to property ...
(c)	deeds and instruments giving a right to recover or receive property ...
It may be that under the new definition control over inflated housing prices could be brought, partly at least, within the purview of the bill. But they would be exempt under the existing definition. That gives rise to a further problem of legislative structure causing confusion not only to members of this House, who for the last two days have tried to come to grips with legislation and attempted to understand what it is supposed to do, but causing confusion in the sense of putting this bill in the framework of the existing Combines Investigation Act and other proposed amendments to that act.
Bill C-7 was introduced in this House first on March 11, and the second reading debate commenced on March 13. It received second reading approval and was referred to the standing committee on finance on April 1. There have been three sessions of the finance committee to deal with the provisions of that bill at which the minister and his colleague have attended to give evidence. Now, we have this bill given first reading in the House on Monday and brought forward for debate today, and it includes some definitional changes when compared to those in Bill C-7. The point is that there is an overlap, and there has been no attempt to coordinate the two pieces of legislation.
Not only do we have that confusion, we have an indication from the government that this Bill C-29 is not going to be referred to the finance committee which is geared up for the next two months to deal with the very complex provisions of Bill C-7. It is to be referred to the justice committee. That is the committee which the government hopes will give it quick and easy treatment. To confuse the matter further, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs last Thursday and again last night indicated that there are further amendments to Bill C-7, some of which will muddy the waters a little more because these amendments to Bill C-7 will have an effect on Bill C-29.
Profiteering Practices
The point of my remarks in this area is to suggest to the government that it should try to pull it all together. The government is confusing members of this House and the people of Canada. If it is going to proceed under the Combines Investigation Act it should present us with a package that has been carefully worked out, giving us some examples of where it is going to apply it, and giving us examples of the sort of mischiefs that it is trying to overcome, and some of the alleged abuses existing in the market place. It should tell us how it will work out, and then let the House of Commons and the people of Canada make their judgment. It should not proceed as it has proceeded with Bill C-29 and Bill C-7, and the amendments to Bill C-7, in this haphazard fashion which gives the appearance at least that someone hurriedly drafted the bill on the weekend preceding the day it was introduced.
The most charitable thing I can say about this bill and the way it was introduced is that it was either put together by somebody who really did not know what he was doing or, alternatively, and this may probably be the case, the form of the legislation was lifted from some wartime legislation introduced in the early 1940's or, indeed, in 1916 or 1917. It looks suspiciously like wartime legislation, and the form is very much akin to what Parliament introduced in that period. Certainly, it is not relevant to the real problems of today.
The hon. member for St. John's East pointed out that the substantive difficulty with this bill is that it represents a form of selective price controls and the focus of the legislation is on profit margins in respect of a particular article or class of articles. This tends to be selective because the choice of products or articles is left up to the governor in council. This may go too far. However here we find the nub of the inconsistency between this bill and the prices and incomes policy that has been recommended by the Progressive Conservative party, because that prices and incomes policy, if the hon. members opposite took the trouble to read what that policy is, focuses only on profit margins in industrial sectors, and it is temporary in nature. It represents a more comprehensive approach which does not attempt to single out or select particular articles of trade or particular products for discriminatory treatment.
Indeed, the nature or scope of the term "industry" could be so broad as to include all processing and manufacturing industries, and it would affect profit margins of those industries only in the broad sense, allowing the price of individual articles or products within those industries to be determined by the people who run the industry and who know best through experience and through vigorous competition in the market place, what will sell and what will not sell, and at what particular price.
Where the role of the government comes in with our prices and incomes policy is in setting reasonable profit margins for a given industrial sector, based not necessarily on the difference between a base year and the subsequent year, which could build in all sorts of inequities for both consumers and businessmen, but based on profit margins measured by return on investment. This may involve a "return on investment" concept which is measured over a much longer period of time than one year. The base year concept which is really the basis of this

May 1, 1974
Profiteering Practices
particular bill, and which will be determined by regulation of the governor in council, may well be a period involving just the year 1973. Indeed, the example which the minister has touted in his press release involves a one-year period, which may be last year, as determining the base year on which profit margins are determined.
What if you have a company, and we have some particularly in the food retailing field, which showed a tremendous profit last year, and that becomes the base year? What this bill suggests to the company is that their profit for that year, will be entrenched into the system and that as long as the company does not exceed that rate in the following year it is okay. But supposing that company in 1973 had been engaging in profiteering and gouging? The mechanism which the government is setting up here might operate to exempt the company from the price freeze and rollback treatment that is proposed by this bill. That is why it is inequitable.
I suggest to hon. members in all seriousness that the bill should not look at particular articles or particular products, but at industrial sectors. The bill should also look at profit margins over the long haul and should key on return on investment. There may be companies that have experienced a loss position for three or four years, and suddenly through changes in the market they may have a good year in terms of profit. That good year may be necessary if that company is to survive, just to recoup its losses for the previous three or four years. One should look at margins over the long haul, and look at them through return on investment. Any governmental agency worth its salt could work with that concept and it is far more equitable.
Quite often not only members of the Liberal party but my friends in the New Democratic Party as well, look at this in an overly simplistic way, taking prices one year and prices the next year, figuring out costs for that very short-term period and arriving at respective profit margins for those years. That is not how the system should work. The system should be based on the concept of return on investment, and it is that concept which determines whether capital is attracted into any industrial sector, whether it be the service sector, the manufacturing sector or the processing sector.
Some mention has been made in the context of this debate of the exemption for agricultural products and fish products. I suppose one really cannot quarrel with these exemptions, except that in this particular bill the existence of exemptions points out the selective nature of the bill. While agricultural producers will be exempt in terms of the products they produce, at the next level up, and I am talking about the distributors of agricultural products, they are going to be subject to the price freeze and rollback regime of government under this bill.
Anybody who knows how a system of this sort has operated in the past, how it has operated in the United States and Great Britain, will know that if the mechanism is invoked in terms of distributors it will only take a matter of a week or two weeks before the freeze or rollback works its way back to the primary producer. Some hon. members opposite may ask: So what? I will tell them "so what". With this bill which is selective in its application the primary producer may find himself frozen in

terms of the price of his product, but he gets hit on the other side because his costs are not frozen. That is the inequitable result of a selective policy of this sort.
That is the reason it is so necessary that any major piece of anti-inflation legislation purporting to authorize price freezes or rollbacks must be comprehensive in nature. It must not be selective. It must cover all aspects of the economy in a broad sense. In case some hon. members might think such a policy as our party has recommended is interventionist in nature, and perhaps as interventionist as the administrative framework which will be set up under this bill, let me again emphasize that it is not necessary to go into an industrial sector and pick out selective products or articles or classes of articles for specific treatment. Indeed, the whole basis of our policy is to preserve the free enterprise system and give it some broad guidelines in terms of return on investment and let it work out its own pricing policy within its own sector. I think our prices and incomes policy is the salvation for business in Canada, small or large, and ultimately the consumer.
I for one would not favour this bill becoming a permanent feature of the statute law of our country. The concepts which were introduced for the first time in this House on Monday are untried and untested. I think at the very minimum, as suggested by the hon. member for St. John's East, there must be some form of parliamentary review. Perhaps we should even consider the concept of a self-destruction clause after a period of one or two years when the bill has had an opportunity to run its course. The point is that Parliament must have an opportunity to look at this sort of legislation if, as appears unlikely, it should pass. This review should be, compulsory because the legislation is dangerous in its delegation of powers to the executive, is untried, and because the minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) today, yesterday and on Monday refused to provide an adequate explanation as to how this legislation will achieve the particular goals that are sought to be achieved and failed to demonstrate an understanding of the nature of the inflationary problem and how to deal with them.
There are some very real, practical legal and substantive difficulties in relation to the specific provisions of this bill. Without wanting to take up too much time I wish to review some of these difficulties because I think it is important that they be placed on the record for Canadians to see. In many respects this bill is an unprecedented delegation of arbitrary power to the executive of this country. Comparisons have been made, suggesting this is almost like wartime legislation, that it is almost like an economic War Measures Act. That may be too strong a comparison. I think it does, however, contain an unprecedented delegation of power which should be of concern to members of this House.
In the first instance, the act may be invoked through the process of a cabinet declaration respecting an article or class of articles. The minister indicated that in the usual case it would be expected that this declaration would not be invoked until after there was a report or recommendation by a body acting under the Inquiries Act such as the Food Prices Review Board. But if one looks at section
May 1, 1974

50(2) one can see that the Governor in Council can circumvent the section whereby the process is initiated by the report of a body under the Inquiries Act. This is the situation where the cabinet can decide that to "await the outcome of such an inquiry and report would not be in the public interest".
In such a case the cabinet could make the declaration unilaterally without the report merely because, in its own opinion certain pricing practices would be likely to have a substantial effect on the price of an article or group of articles which would seriously affect the living cost of a majority of Canadians. That is a pretty fantastic power. Some may say there is a time limit, and that a declaration is effective only a year. However, in section 50(3) one can see there is a possibility of an extension for a period not exceeding six months. However, that is for only one order for extension. If one reads the section closely it is clear that there could be one for six months and a second order for another six months. It would be very easy for the cabinet unilaterally to keep that declaration in place ad infinitum; in other words, to provide a permanent measure of control for a certain article or class of articles. This is getting as close to a managed economy as one can get all in one fell swoop.
I think that would be a dangerous situation and one which would be seriously debated. I have another concern that the government can exempt any class or classes of persons or transactions from the 30-day reporting requirement under section 52. No standards or guidelines are given concerning the conditions or criteria under which such exemptions could be granted. Would the exemptions be granted to certain industries dealing in products subject to a declaration because they were in financial difficulty and should be allowed to increase their prices without having to give notice to the Director under section 51, or would it more likely be the case that only the friends of the government could secure an exemption.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I think this House would like to have drawn to its attention that approximately one and a half hours ago a former member of this House for many years, and a public servant in Canada for most of his life, passed away, George Doucett. George Doucett was born on May 16, 1897. He was first elected to the Ontario House in 1936. He was re-elected in 1943, 1945, 1948, 1951 and 1955. As a minister of the Crown, he was first appointed in 1943 and re-appointed in 1948, 1949 and 1955 as Minister of Highways and Public Works in the province of Ontario. He resigned in order to run for the House of Commons and was first elected in 1957. He was subsequently elected in 1958 and in 1962. He passed away in Carleton Place an hour and a half ago. I call this to the attention of the House.
